title: Databricks Apps and application architecture
summary: One request, three trust boundaries: a Databricks App's front end, back end and data path, the identity chosen at each hop, and where state, secrets and checks must live before anything is deployed.
outcomes: Trace a request from browser to data, model or tool through a Databricks App's front end and back end, naming the trust boundary and identity at each hop.
Choose app authorization or user authorization per request, bind resources and secrets without credentials in code, and read user context only from the platform's headers.
Place every piece of application state where it must survive, pin dependencies, and assign each rule to its enforcement point with request validation first.
Assign incident ownership by evidence, and write mocked contract tests and a deployment guide that state exactly what they prove and label what was not deployed.
startingAssumptions: The cloud bridge and the trust-boundary lesson have covered DNS, identity and authorization on one request.
Unity Catalog privileges are familiar from the governance module, and basic Python and HTTP request and response ideas are familiar.
editorialRationale: Application teaching fails when it starts from a framework or a database, so the module follows one fictional request through its three trust boundaries, makes the identity at each hop a per-request decision, then treats resources, secrets and user context as separate facts before placing state by class. Runtime, dependencies, validation, enforcement points, operations and deployment follow in the order an architecture review asks for them, and the module ends on what a local mock can and cannot prove. Every platform detail that could not be re-confirmed in this build is marked for verification rather than stated as settled.

concepts.definition: A web application that Databricks hosts on managed serverless compute inside a workspace, reached at its own URL after the platform signs the user in.
concepts.example: Cinderline's quality exception review app, a FastAPI back end serving a small front end to reviewers.

concepts.definition: The hops one request crosses: browser to the platform's sign-in, platform to the app's back end, and back end to each data, model or tool service.
concepts.example: Claim: browser → sign-in → back end → Lakebase quality_ops, three boundaries.

concepts.definition: The dedicated, non-reusable identity Databricks creates for one app, whose permissions are evaluated for every call the app makes under app authorization.
concepts.example: The queue query appears in query history under the quality app's principal, not under Leo.

concepts.definition: An app authorization mode in which the back end calls Databricks with the signed-in user's forwarded access token, so the user's own permissions apply.
concepts.example: With user authorization, Imani's row filter on the quarantine table decides which rows her queue shows.

concepts.definition: A declared limit on the Databricks APIs a user-authorized app may call on a user's behalf, enforced even when the user holds broader permissions.
concepts.example: The quality app declares only sql, so it cannot read workspace files for Imani.

concepts.definition: The identity facts the platform forwards with each request, read by the back end per request and never taken from the client-controlled body.
concepts.example: X-Forwarded-Email: imani.q@cinderline.example becomes reviewer imani.q on the claim row.

concepts.definition: A workspace object added to an app with a permission for the app's service principal and a key that app.yaml maps to an environment variable.
concepts.example: Key sql-warehouse, permission Can use, variable QUALITY_WAREHOUSE_ID.

concepts.definition: A secret added to an app as a resource so the process receives its value through an environment variable instead of from source or configuration.
concepts.example: quality-app/manuals-token reaches the process as MANUALS_TOKEN.

concepts.definition: A classification of each value an app holds by what must be true after the request ends, which decides where it may live.
concepts.example: A claim is operational and lives in Lakebase; a filter is session state and may live in the browser.

concepts.definition: The platform-managed compute that runs the app's start command as a process, which a deployment or restart replaces with a new one.
concepts.example: Deployment 8 starts a new process with empty memory while Lakebase keeps every claim.

concepts.definition: The files a deployment reads to install the app's packages, which decide the versions the running app actually gets.
concepts.example: qa-rules==1.4 in requirements.txt makes the build install the tested version.

concepts.definition: The checks a back end applies to a request's body and parameters before any handler runs under a privileged identity.
concepts.example: inspection_key must match ^[A-Z]-\d{4}$, so A-2031' OR '1'='1 is refused with a 422.

concepts.definition: The one place in the request path that is responsible for refusing a particular rule, chosen by who can see the facts the rule needs.
concepts.example: The plant rule is enforced in the handler; one active claim is enforced by Lakebase.

concepts.definition: The agreed split of which team owns which failure, decided by which layer's evidence shows the fault.
concepts.example: A failed install is the app team's; a query queued behind a refresh is the warehouse owner's.

concepts.definition: The replayable sequence that turns synced source files into the running app: deploy, build, start, verify and share.
concepts.example: Sync the folder, deploy it, read the install step, open the URL, share with the reviewers' group.

concepts.definition: Configuration that declares an app and the resources it uses so the same deployment repeats per target, such as development and production.
concepts.example: A bundle target dev binds wh-quality-dev; target prod binds wh-quality.

concepts.definition: A local test that drives the real handler with fakes in place of its dependencies to prove its request, response and error contract, and nothing about a deployment.
concepts.example: FakeClaims returns claimed then conflict while a test client posts two claims.

concepts.definition: The Postgres role a Lakebase binding gives an app's service principal, with database-level privileges but no automatic rights on existing tables.

questions.prompt: Imani's browser developer tools show one request for her claim, POST /v1/claims to the app URL, and nothing else. Where did the Lakebase insert for that claim come from?

options.text: From the app's back end process, after the request arrived; the browser only ever talks to the app URL.
options.rationale: Correct: the back end is the only party that calls data services, using an identity the app is configured with.

options.text: From the browser, through a second request that developer tools hide.
options.rationale: Developer tools show every request the page makes; a browser holding a database connection would also hold a credential.

options.text: From the platform's sign-in service, which writes the body to Lakebase itself.
options.rationale: Sign-in authenticates and forwards; it has no knowledge of the app's tables or rules.

options.text: From Lakebase, which polls the app for pending claims.
options.rationale: Databases answer connections; they do not poll applications for work.

questions.prompt: Leo holds no grant on quality.raw.quarantine, yet under app authorization the queue page shows him open items. What explains this, and what must the design add?

options.text: The query runs as the app's service principal, which holds SELECT; the handler must narrow results to Leo's plants because Unity Catalog never evaluates Leo.
options.rationale: Correct: under app authorization the principal at the data hop is the app, so per-reviewer narrowing is the app's job.

options.text: Leo inherited the app owner's grants when he opened the app, so nothing needs adding.
options.rationale: An app's reach is its own service principal's grants; the owner's personal grants never travel with it.

options.text: The platform grants SELECT to every user who may open an app, so row filters will narrow it.
options.rationale: Permission to open an app grants nothing on data, and a filter is evaluated for the app's principal here.

options.text: The warehouse replays results cached from Imani's session, so clearing the cache fixes it.
options.rationale: Results are computed per query under the calling principal; a cache is not the cause of this behaviour.

questions.prompt: The application state design guide's ClaimRequest example carries a reviewer field. In the running app, which source should decide the reviewer recorded on the claim row?

options.text: The identity header the platform forwards after sign-in; a body value that disagrees is refused.
options.rationale: Correct: the platform sets the header after authentication, while any client can write any body.

options.text: The body's reviewer field, because it is part of the versioned contract.
options.rationale: A contract field describes the record; it cannot prove who sent the request, since the client writes it.

options.text: A cookie the front end sets when the page loads.
options.rationale: A cookie written by front end code is client-controlled, exactly like the body.

options.text: The reviewer of the previous request, kept in a module-level variable.
options.rationale: Concurrent requests from different reviewers share module-level variables, so this records the wrong person.

questions.prompt: In production every queue request fails with PERMISSION_DENIED naming the app's principal on quality.raw.quarantine. The warehouse is bound as a resource with Can use. What is missing?

options.text: Unity Catalog privileges for the app's service principal on the catalog, schema and table; Can use on a warehouse grants compute, not data.
options.rationale: Correct: the binding lets the app run queries on the warehouse; reading the table still needs its own grants.

options.text: A second warehouse binding with Can manage, which includes data access.
options.rationale: Managing a warehouse governs the compute resource, never the tables queried through it.

options.text: Imani's SELECT grant, because the app runs every query as the signed-in user.
options.rationale: The error names the app's principal, so the query ran under app authorization.

options.text: The warehouse ID pasted into app.yaml as a literal value instead of valueFrom.
options.rationale: How the ID reaches the process does not change which grants the principal holds.

questions.prompt: Five minutes after the manuals token was rotated (the new value stored in the secret scope and the old token revoked at the manuals service), manual text fails with 401 while claims and the queue still work. What is the most likely cause and the next step?

options.text: The running process still holds the value it read at start; restart or redeploy the app and confirm with the next manual request.
options.rationale: Correct: an injected environment variable is read once per process, so a rotation needs a new process.

options.text: The rotation removed the resource's Can read permission; add the secret resource again.
options.rationale: Storing a new value in the scope does not change the app's permission on that secret.

options.text: Imani's forwarded token expired; ask her to sign in again.
options.rationale: The manuals call uses the bound secret, not the reviewer's token, and other requests still work.

options.text: The warehouse is overloaded; increase its size.
options.rationale: The failing call goes to the manuals service and returns 401, an authentication answer, not a capacity one.

questions.prompt: The team redeployed a fix at 12:00. At 12:05 Leo claims A-2031 revision 2 successfully, although Imani claimed it at 11:40. Where was Imani's claim most likely stored?

options.text: In a dictionary in the app process's memory, which the redeploy replaced with an empty one.
options.rationale: Correct: a deployment starts a new process, and process memory is never carried across.

options.text: In Lakebase, which the redeploy truncated.
options.rationale: Deploying an app changes its code and process, not the rows in a separate database.

options.text: In the browser's local storage, which Leo's browser shares.
options.rationale: Browser storage belongs to one browser profile; Leo's browser cannot read Imani's.

options.text: In the morning summary table, which refreshes hourly.
options.rationale: The summary is derived from operational records; it is never where a claim is written.

questions.prompt: The app runs on a laptop, but the deployment log ends with ImportError: cannot import name 'parse_key' from 'qa_rules'. requirements.txt lists qa-rules with no version. What is the best first fix?

options.text: Pin qa-rules to the version the tests ran against and redeploy; the build resolved a newer release.
options.rationale: Correct: the deployment installs from the manifest, so an unpinned line takes whatever is current that day.

options.text: Copy the laptop's site-packages folder into the app folder.
options.rationale: Installed packages are platform-specific and bypass the manifest the build reads; the build still decides.

options.text: Grant the app's service principal Can manage on the SQL warehouse.
options.rationale: An ImportError happens before any warehouse call; permissions cannot change which package was installed.

options.text: Add qa_rules to the env list in app.yaml.
options.rationale: The env list sets environment variables; it does not install or select Python packages.

questions.prompt: Suppose the schema check were removed but the queue query still binds inspection_key as a parameter. What does the injected body A-2031' OR '1'='1 produce?

options.text: No rows and no field error: the whole string is compared as one literal key value.
options.rationale: Correct: a bound parameter is never parsed as SQL, so the quote and OR clause are just characters.

options.text: Every plant's rows, because parameters are pasted into the text before execution.
options.rationale: That describes concatenation; binding sends the value separately from the statement text.

options.text: A 422 naming inspection_key, because the warehouse validates key patterns.
options.rationale: The warehouse knows nothing of the app's contract; only the removed schema produced a 422.

options.text: A 401, because the platform's sign-in detects injection attempts.
options.rationale: Sign-in authenticates the reviewer and does not inspect request bodies at all.

questions.prompt: Imani and Leo press Claim on A-2031 revision 2 within the same 50 milliseconds, and the two requests reach different processes. Which check guarantees that only one of them succeeds?

options.text: The database's one-active-claim rule, because only the store sees both writes.
options.rationale: Correct: each process sees only its own request; the store serializes the two inserts against one rule.

options.text: The handler's in-memory check that the item is unclaimed, because it runs first.
options.rationale: Each process has its own memory, so both checks can see 'unclaimed' at the same moment.

options.text: The schema check, because the second body duplicates the first.
options.rationale: Both bodies are individually valid; a schema judges one request's shape, never other requests.

options.text: The platform's sign-in, which serializes requests for each app.
options.rationale: Sign-in authenticates each request independently and imposes no ordering on writes.

questions.prompt: The five mocked contract tests pass. Which statement can the team put in the architecture review note without overclaiming?

options.text: The handler returns claimed, conflict, 422 and 403 as specified when its dependencies behave like the fakes.
options.rationale: Correct: that is exactly what driving the real handler against fakes demonstrates, and no more.

options.text: The app's service principal can read quality.raw.quarantine.
options.rationale: The warehouse was replaced by a fake, so no grant was exercised.

options.text: Two concurrent claims on the same item cannot both succeed in Lakebase.
options.rationale: The fake store runs one request at a time; concurrency needs a real database test.

options.text: The platform forwards X-Forwarded-Email to this app.
options.rationale: The tests set that header themselves; only a deployed app shows what the platform sends.

selfQuestions.prompt: The data lead confirms that a per-plant row filter now exists on quality.raw.quarantine. Rewrite the view-queue trace, say what the handler no longer has to do, what it still must do, and what you would test before release.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: The queue read now calls the warehouse with Imani's forwarded token and only the sql scope, so Unity Catalog's row filter limits the quarantine rows to her plants and the handler no longer filters those rows. Before the switch the reviewers' group is granted USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and SELECT on quality.raw.quarantine, and the warehouse owner confirms whether reviewers also need Can use on the warehouse; without those grants a reviewer such as Leo gets a permission error. The handler still reads claims from Lakebase as the app and must narrow them to her plants, still checks plant membership before a claim, and must never cache query results across reviewers. Test with two reviewers from different plants, one newly added reviewer who must see rows rather than an error, and one person outside the reviewers' group with no grant, read the principal in query history, and confirm a missing token is refused rather than silently falling back to the app.
selfQuestions.reasoning: The trace changes only at the hop whose data carries per-user rules; writes keep the app's identity because reviewers hold no Lakebase grants. Checking the principal in query history catches a silent fallback, which the agent authentication page warns about; keeping handler filtering as defence in depth is an acceptable alternative.

selfQuestions.prompt: A colleague argues that because the quality app runs as a single process today, keeping active claims in a dictionary is acceptable. Give two events that break it without any change to scaling, and say what you would read in the documentation before accepting any in-memory state.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: A redeploy starts a new process with empty memory, so every open claim disappears and a second reviewer can claim the same item; a restart after a crash or a platform-initiated restart does the same, with no deployment at all. Before accepting in-memory state I would read the current environment and compute documentation for how processes are started, restarted and sized, and whether more than one can serve an app, and I would still keep claims in Lakebase because the design must be correct in every case.
selfQuestions.reasoning: The argument fails on process lifetime, not only on instance count: any event that replaces the process loses memory. Naming a crash restart and a deployment is enough; mentioning a future second process is an acceptable third reason.

selfQuestions.prompt: Reviewers report a blank queue since 09:10. Write the first three evidence items you would read, in order, and name the owner after each.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: First, the deployment history and app log around 09:10: a deployment or restart at that moment makes it the app team's. Second, the app log's queue requests: an exception, a 401 or 403 from a data call, or an empty result with no error. Third, if a data call was refused, the grant on the named object and the principal it names, which hands it to the data owner; if the call was slow or empty, the warehouse's query history, which hands it to the warehouse owner.
selfQuestions.reasoning: The order starts at the layer the team controls and moves outward only on evidence, so no owner is paged on a guess. Starting with the warehouse query history is acceptable when the app log already shows the time spent there.

selfQuestions.prompt: Write the deployment guide for the quality app as numbered steps, each with the evidence that proves it happened, and state the label the guide carries before anyone runs it.
selfQuestions.modelAnswer: 1. Create the app and bind sql-warehouse, quality-db and manuals-token with their permissions: evidence, the app's resource list. 2. Sync the folder: evidence, the files in the workspace folder. 3. Deploy: evidence, a new deployment in the history. 4. Build: evidence, the install step listing the pinned versions. 5. Start: evidence, the first app log lines. 6. Verify: evidence, the URL opens and Imani's test claim appears in Lakebase. 7. Share with the reviewers' group. The guide is labelled not deployed until someone runs it and records each result.
selfQuestions.reasoning: Each step is paired with evidence a second person can check, so the guide is replayable and its status is honest; ordering resource bindings after the first deploy is an acceptable alternative if the first deploy only serves a health page.

beats.title: A browser reaches the app URL, never the warehouse
beats.outcome: Trace one request through the browser, the platform's sign-in, the app's front end and back end, and the data, model or tool it calls.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-apps-app-concept|Databricks App]] is a web application the platform hosts on managed serverless compute beside the data. Its front end runs in the reviewer's browser: pages and scripts that hold no data credential. Its back end is the server process your code defines, and it alone calls the SQL warehouse, Lakebase, a serving endpoint or an outside tool. Notice in the second state that a claim travels browser, sign-in, back end, Lakebase, and the browser never meets a data service.

handbook.markdown:
The documentation lists Python frameworks (Streamlit, Dash, Gradio, Flask, FastAPI) and Node.js frameworks (React, Angular, Svelte, Express). They differ in where the page is assembled, not in where your code runs. Streamlit, Dash and Gradio build the page from Python and keep a live connection to the server; a React or plain HTML front end is a set of static files that call JSON endpoints. Either way the code that holds credentials runs in the back end process on Databricks-managed compute.

Three boundaries sit on every request, and each has a different owner:

| Boundary | Who is checked | What decides |
|---|---|---|
| Browser → platform | the reviewer | the platform's sign-in and the app's permission |
| Platform → back end | nothing new | the platform forwards identity headers |
| Back end → data, model, tool | the identity the app chooses | grants on that object |

```python
# Synthetic teaching example; not executed.
@app.get("/v1/queue")
def queue(request: Request):
    reviewer = reviewer_of(request)          # from the forwarded headers
    items = deps.open_items(plants=deps.plants_of(reviewer))
    return {"reviewer": reviewer, "items": items}
```

**Why use it:** the data stays in the workspace, sign-in is the workspace's own, and resources are bound with permissions rather than pasted credentials. **When not:** a public audience with no Databricks identity, long-running batch computation (a job owns that), or a question a dashboard or Genie Agent (formerly Genie space) already answers without custom code.

**What to inspect:** the browser's network panel shows requests only to the app URL; the warehouse's query history shows which principal ran each query. If a browser ever holds a token for a data service, the path is wrong.

beats.recap: The browser reaches the app; only the back end reaches data, models and tools.
beats.changeNote: The handbook now uses the name Databricks' documentation gives this feature, Genie Agent (formerly Genie space); the advice is unchanged. Source: Databricks' developer documentation, Genie Agents page (databricks/devhub at commit 35f4745).

beats.title: Under app authorization the warehouse sees the app, not the reviewer
beats.outcome: Say which principal a data service evaluates under app authorization and under user authorization, and what that means for a reviewer without grants.
beats.explanation: Every app gets a dedicated [[dbxfe-apps-principal-concept|app service principal]], unique to that app, and the platform injects its credentials into the process. Under app authorization the warehouse and Lakebase evaluate that principal, so Leo, who holds no grant on the quarantine table, sees whatever the app's grant returns unless the handler narrows it. Under [[dbxfe-apps-userauth-concept|user authorization]] the back end forwards Imani's token and the warehouse evaluates Imani. Notice that the row-filter node is evaluated in both states, first for the app and then for Imani.

samajh.text: Socho ek society building hai. Maintenance staff ke paas society ki master key hai. Imani staff ko bolti hai 'mera parcel store room se laa do'; staff society ki key se darwaza kholta hai, isliye staff ko khud dekhna padta hai ki Imani ko woh parcel lene ka haq hai ya nahi. Doosra tareeka: Imani apni flat ki chaabi deti hai, sirf is ek kaam ke liye. Tab darwaza wahi khulega jo Imani ke liye khulta hai, usse zyada nahi.
samajh.mapping: The society's master key is the app's service principal, the resident's own key lent for one errand is the forwarded user token, and 'only this errand' is the declared scope.
samajh.boundary: A token expires and is scoped by the app's declaration, not by the resident's wish; and unlike a key, it must never be copied, stored or reused for another resident.

handbook.markdown:
The service principal is created with the app and cannot be reused by another app. Databricks injects its OAuth credentials as `DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID` and `DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET`; the Databricks SDK's `Config()` reads them from the environment, while the SQL connector does not, so `query_as_app` below passes the SDK's credentials to it through `credentials_provider`. Grants are made to that principal like any other: warehouse permission through the app's resources, Unity Catalog privileges on the tables it reads, a Postgres role on Lakebase.

```python
# Synthetic teaching example; not executed. Check the current connector and SDK docs.
from databricks import sql
from databricks.sdk.core import Config
cfg = Config()   # inside the app: host and the app's injected credentials

def query_as_app(http_path, statement, params):
    with sql.connect(server_hostname=cfg.host, http_path=http_path,
                     credentials_provider=lambda: cfg.authenticate) as conn:
        with conn.cursor() as cur:
            cur.execute(statement, params)
            return cur.fetchall()

def query_as_user(request, http_path, statement, params):
    token = request.headers.get("x-forwarded-access-token")  # user authorization only
    with sql.connect(server_hostname=cfg.host, http_path=http_path,
                     access_token=token) as conn:
        with conn.cursor() as cur:
            cur.execute(statement, params)
            return cur.fetchall()
```

**Consequences.** Under app authorization the audit trail at the data hop names the app, so the app must record the reviewer itself: on the claim row and in its own log line with the request. Row filters and column masks are evaluated on every access for whichever principal runs the query; written for reviewers, they are evaluated for the app's principal under app authorization and cannot narrow its results to one reviewer. Under user authorization the reviewer's grants, filters and masks apply, and a reviewer without SELECT gets a permission error, which the front end must present plainly.

**What to inspect:** the principal column of the warehouse's query history for one queue request. If it names the app when you expected Imani, the forwarded token was not used.

beats.recap: App authorization makes the app the caller; user authorization makes the reviewer the caller.
beats.changeNote: Two corrections; no check's answer changed. The diagram and handbook now say a row filter on the table is evaluated for the app's principal under app authorization, not skipped (Databricks' developer documentation, Read Unity Catalog tables, databricks/devhub at 35f4745). The handbook now says the SDK's Config() reads the injected credentials but the SQL connector does not (source of Databricks SDK for Python v0.141.0 and SQL Connector 4.6.0).

beats.title: User authorization is bounded by the reviewer's grants and the app's scopes
beats.outcome: Choose app or user authorization per request, name the scope a user-authorized call needs, and state how the forwarded token must be handled.
beats.explanation: User authorization narrows twice. The warehouse applies Imani's own grants, and the app may act for her only within the [[dbxfe-apps-scope-concept|scopes]] it declared, such as sql; anything outside them is blocked even if Imani could do it in a notebook. Choose per request, not per app: in the table, the queue read moves to Imani's token only once a row filter exists, while claims and dispositions stay with the app. The forwarded token lives for one request: never store it, log it or share it.

handbook.markdown:
**Status first.** The agent authentication page reviewed for this course marked user authorization Public Preview, and the authorization page describes it as something the app declares with scopes. Before designing on it, confirm its current status and whether it must be enabled for the workspace; if it is unavailable, the app-identity design with handler filtering is the fallback, not an afterthought.

**Scopes bound the app, not the person.** A scope such as `sql` lets the app run warehouse queries as the user. Adding a feature that needs another API means declaring another scope, which widens what the app can do on everyone's behalf; review it as a permission change, not a code change.

**Token handling rules** (original guidance):

- Read `X-Forwarded-Access-Token` from the current request and pass it straight to the call that needs it.
- Never write it to a log, a database, a cache key or a module-level variable; one global holding "the current token" serves one reviewer's rights to another reviewer's concurrent request.
- If the header is missing on a request that must run as the user, refuse with 401. The agent authentication page warns that a missing token can fall back to app identity; a silent fallback turns a per-user read into the app's wider read.
- Never cache user-authorized results under a key that ignores the user.

**Moving a read to the user moves its grants too.** Under app authorization Leo needs no grant on `quality.raw.quarantine`; once the queue read runs on his token, the warehouse evaluates Leo, so the reviewers' group needs USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and SELECT on the table, and the warehouse owner confirms whether reviewers also need Can use on `wh-quality`. Grant before the switch, and test that a newly added reviewer sees rows, not an error.

**Mixing is normal.** One app can read with the user's token where the data carries per-user rules and write with its own identity where reviewers hold no grants. Write the choice per request in the design note, as the table does, with the enforcement point beside it.

**What to inspect:** the app's declared scopes, the principal in query history for one request per reviewer, and a test with a reviewer who holds no grant: she must see an error, not the app's rows.

beats.recap: Choose the identity per request; a user token is bounded by the user's grants and the app's scopes.

beats.title: Who is asking comes from the platform's headers, never from the body
beats.outcome: Read the reviewer's identity from forwarded headers, refuse a body that names someone else, and record the reviewer on the rows the app writes.
beats.explanation: After sign-in, the platform forwards the reviewer's [[dbxfe-apps-context-concept|user context]] to the back end in request headers such as X-Forwarded-Email. The browser controls the JSON body, so a body field naming a reviewer is an assertion, not evidence. The application state design guide's ClaimRequest carries reviewer; the back end fills it from the header and refuses a body value that disagrees. Notice in the forged state that the handler refuses before any row is written, and that the header did not change.

handbook.markdown:
The header names used here, `X-Forwarded-Email` and `X-Forwarded-User`, are as the author recalled them from the Apps documentation's header page, not re-read in this build, whose URL was not confirmed in this build: read the current list before relying on a name, and confirm there that the platform replaces a same-named header a client tries to send.

```python
# Synthetic teaching example; not executed.
from fastapi import HTTPException, Request

def reviewer_of(request: Request) -> str:
    email = request.headers.get("x-forwarded-email")
    if not email:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=401, detail={"reason": "identity"})
    return email.split("@")[0]          # imani.q

@app.post("/v1/claims")
def claim(body: ClaimRequest, request: Request):
    reviewer = reviewer_of(request)
    if body.reviewer not in (None, reviewer):
        raise HTTPException(status_code=403, detail={"reason": "reviewer"})
    ...
```

**Three rules for user context** (original guidance):

1. **Per request.** Read it inside the handler every time. A module-level `CURRENT_REVIEWER` in a server that handles concurrent requests records one reviewer's claim under another's name.
2. **From the platform.** Headers the platform sets after authentication are the only identity evidence the back end has. The body, query string, cookies and front end state are all written by the client.
3. **Recorded.** Under app authorization the data services see the app, so the reviewer, the request id and the time go on the row and in the log line. Without them, the audit trail ends at "the app did it".

Locally there is no platform in front of the app, so tests set these headers by hand. That proves the handler reads them correctly and nothing about whether the platform sends them; the mock beat returns to that gap.

beats.recap: Identity comes from platform headers per request; the body can only agree or be refused.

beats.title: A resource binding is a grant plus an injected value
beats.outcome: Write the resource table for an app: each resource, its key, the permission for the app's principal and the variable the code reads.
beats.explanation: Adding an [[dbxfe-apps-binding-concept|app resource]] does two things at once: it grants the app's service principal a chosen permission on a workspace object, and it gives that object a key that app.yaml maps to an environment variable with valueFrom. The code reads QUALITY_WAREHOUSE_ID, never a pasted ID or credential. Notice in the second state that promotion to production changes only what four keys resolve to; app.yaml and the code stay the same.

handbook.markdown:
The resources page lists the object types an app can use, including SQL warehouses, model serving endpoints, secrets, jobs, Unity Catalog volumes and Lakebase databases, and the permission choices for each; pick the narrowest one that works, such as *Can use* for a warehouse the app only queries and *Can query* for an endpoint it only calls.

```yaml
# app.yaml; synthetic teaching example, keys checked against the current page. Not deployed.
command: ["uvicorn", "server:app"]      # plus the host and port options the environment page specifies
env:
  - name: QUALITY_WAREHOUSE_ID
    valueFrom: sql-warehouse
  - name: MANUALS_TOKEN
    valueFrom: manuals-token
```

**A binding is not every grant.** Can use on the warehouse lets the app's principal run statements on that compute; reading `quality.raw.quarantine` still needs Unity Catalog privileges on the catalog, schema and table (the Unity Catalog module teaches that privilege model). A Lakebase binding gives the principal a matching Postgres role with CONNECT and CREATE on the chosen database and injects connection variables such as `PGHOST`; tables the app did not create need their own grants, which the module *Lakebase, Postgres and operational state* designs.

**Why keys and not IDs:** the same app.yaml runs in development and production because each workspace binds its own objects to the same keys, and nobody pastes a warehouse path or a password into configuration.

**Diagnosis order for a denial:** read which principal the error names; list the app's resources and their permissions; then list the grants on the object the error names. A denial naming the app is a grant question, never a code question.

beats.recap: Bind each resource once, with the narrowest permission, and read it through its key.

beats.title: A secret is bound, read at start and never printed
beats.outcome: Keep a credential out of source, app.yaml and logs, and predict what a rotation does to a running app.
beats.explanation: The manuals service needs a token. It lives in a secret scope and reaches the app as a [[dbxfe-apps-secret-concept|secret resource]]: the app's principal gets read permission and app.yaml maps MANUALS_TOKEN to the resource key. The process reads it from its environment when it starts. Notice in the second state what that implies: after the 10:00 rotation, which also revoked the old token at the service, the running process still sends the old value and the call fails until a restart or redeploy starts a process that reads the new one.

samajh.text: Guest ghar aaya, toh aapne darwaze par hi Wi-Fi ka password ek card par likh ke de diya. Woh poori shaam wahi password use karta hai. Beech mein aapne router ka password badal diya, toh guest ka phone baar baar fail hoga, jab tak koi use naya card na de. Aur card ki photo kisi group mein post ho gayi, toh password sabka ho gaya.
samajh.mapping: The card handed over at the door is the environment variable read at process start, changing the router password is a rotation, handing a new card is a restart, and the posted photo is a secret printed to a log.
samajh.boundary: A process cannot ask for a new card on its own; only a restart or redeploy re-reads the value, and the platform, not a person, hands it over.

handbook.markdown:
**Where a credential may appear:** in the secret scope, and in the memory of the process that uses it. Nowhere else: not in source, Git history, app.yaml `value:` entries, the front end, error pages or logs.

```python
# Synthetic teaching example; not executed.
import logging, os, httpx
log = logging.getLogger("quality")
MANUALS_TOKEN = os.environ["MANUALS_TOKEN"]      # read once, at process start

def manual_text(key: str) -> str:
    r = httpx.get(f"https://manuals.cinderline.example/v1/{key}",
                  headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {MANUALS_TOKEN}"}, timeout=5)
    log.info("manual fetch", extra={"key": key, "status": r.status_code})  # never the token
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.text
```

**The environment holds more than your secret.** Databricks also injects `DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID` and `DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET`, the app's own credentials. A start-up line that prints `os.environ`, or an error page that dumps settings, publishes the app's identity to everyone who can read the logs. Log key names, never values.

**Rotation is a deployment event** (original guidance): because the value is read at start, rotating a secret is complete only when every process serving the app has restarted. Plan it: store the new value, restart or redeploy, watch the next outbound call succeed, then revoke the old value at the service. Revoking first causes exactly the 401 in the timeline.

**When not to use a secret resource:** for the app's own access to Databricks objects. The app's principal and its resource permissions already cover that; a personal access token stored as a secret would make the app act as a person and bypass the design.

**What to inspect:** the app's resource list (is the secret bound with read permission?), a search of the repository and app.yaml for the literal value, and the log lines around the first outbound call after a rotation.

beats.recap: Bind secrets, read them at start, log names not values, and restart after rotation.

beats.title: Process memory belongs to one process and one deployment
beats.outcome: Classify each value the app holds and place it where it must survive, naming what breaks on a second process or after a redeploy.
beats.explanation: Classify [[dbxfe-apps-state-concept|state]] by what must be true after the request ends. A claim must be visible to every reviewer, on any process serving the app, after any redeploy, so it belongs in Lakebase, the store the module Lakebase, Postgres and operational state designs. A filter may live in the browser; manual text may be a cache with expiry; a token is never stored. Notice in the first state that a claim in process A's memory is invisible to process B and gone at the next deployment.

samajh.text: Office mein do ek jaise meeting rooms hain. Imani Room A ke whiteboard par likhti hai 'A-2031 maine le liya'. Leo Room B mein baitha hai, usse kuch nahi dikhta, aur raat ko safai wale dono boards mita dete hain. Agar wahi baat corridor ke shared notice board par likhi hoti, toh dono rooms se dikhti aur agle din bhi rehti.
samajh.mapping: Each meeting room's whiteboard is one process's memory, the nightly cleaning is a redeploy or restart, and the shared corridor notice board is the operational store in Lakebase.
samajh.boundary: A notice board only displays; Lakebase also enforces rules such as one active claim per item, so two people cannot both write 'mine' at the same moment.

handbook.markdown:
The five classes come from the application state design guide, and only one of them needs transactions:

| Class | Example | Needs transactions | Store |
|---|---|---|---|
| Per-request | forwarded token, request id | No | the request only |
| Session | queue filter | No | browser or session cache |
| Operational | claims, dispositions | Yes | Lakebase `quality_ops` |
| Derived analytical | morning summary | No | Delta table, refreshed hourly |
| Cache | manual text | No | process memory with expiry |

**Operational state carries invariants,** and the store, not the handler, must enforce them: at most one active claim per inspection key and revision; a disposition only by the current claimant, changing the disposition and the item's status together; dispositions appended, never updated. The module *Lakebase, Postgres and operational state* turns those into constraints and tests them against a real Postgres; this module only decides that they live there.

**Why memory fails even with one process** (original guidance): a deployment starts a new process, a restart does the same, and if more than one process ever serves the app, each has its own memory. Whatever the current documentation says about instance counts, a design that is correct only while exactly one long-lived process exists is wrong.

**Synchronization is stated, not implied.** Dispositions reach the analytical table hourly; the dashboard prints "dispositions as of 07:00", and a reviewer who needs the live queue uses the app.

**Caches are safe only when losing them costs a recompute.** Key a cache by everything its value depends on; under user authorization that includes the user, or the cache serves one reviewer's rows to another.

**What to inspect:** search the code for module-level dictionaries, lists and globals written by handlers; each one is either a cache with an expiry or a bug.

beats.recap: Put each value where it must survive: claims in Lakebase, filters in the browser, tokens nowhere.

beats.title: The platform runs the process; the team owns what it runs
beats.outcome: Separate what the managed runtime provides from what the app team owns, and predict what survives a restart or redeploy.
beats.explanation: Databricks Apps runs your app on serverless compute that Databricks provisions and manages: nobody on the team sizes a cluster or patches a machine. What runs there is yours: the start command, the [[dbxfe-apps-runtime-concept|process]] it starts, its dependencies and where its state goes. Notice in the second state that a redeploy starts a new process whose memory is empty while Lakebase still holds twelve open claims. Compute size and any scaling options are read from the current documentation; the design must be correct either way.

handbook.markdown:
**What the platform provides:** the compute the app runs on, the sign-in in front of the app URL, the injected identity and resource variables, and starting the process with your command at each deployment.

**What the team owns:** the code, the command in app.yaml, the dependency manifest, request validation, the handler's authorization checks, where each piece of state lives, what the app logs and how failures are reported to reviewers.

**Read, do not assume, the environment.** The app environment page, linked from the overview and not confirmed in this build, documents the operating system and language versions, pre-installed libraries, the compute size choices and the variables the platform sets, including the port the app must serve on (`DATABRICKS_APP_PORT`, as the author recalled it; not re-read in this build). These change between releases; record the values on the date you read them.

**Design rule** (original guidance): correctness must not depend on the lifetime or number of processes. Test it by asking three questions of every value a handler writes:

1. If this process restarts now, what is lost?
2. If a second process served the next request, would it see this?
3. If the next deployment happens mid-shift, what do reviewers notice?

Operational records fail all three in memory, which is why they live in Lakebase.

**When not to use an app process:** heavy or long computations such as recomputing the morning summary for every plant. Run those as a job on a schedule and let the app read the result; a request should finish in seconds, and a page waiting on a batch computation fails whenever the process is replaced.

**What to inspect:** the deployment history (when was the process last replaced?), the app log's first lines after each start, and whether any reviewer-visible behaviour changed at that moment.

beats.recap: Databricks runs and replaces the process; the team owns the command, the code and where state lives.

beats.title: Dependencies are resolved at deployment, not copied from a laptop
beats.outcome: Write the manifest and app.yaml so the deployed build installs the versions you tested and starts the command you intend.
beats.explanation: Packages installed on a laptop never travel with the app. At deployment the build installs what requirements.txt lists, or package.json for Node.js, runs a build script if one is defined, then runs the start command from app.yaml. An unpinned line resolves to whatever is current on the day. Notice in the first state that qa-rules resolved to 2.0 while the tests ran on 1.4, so the start fails; pinning in the second state makes the build install the tested [[dbxfe-apps-dependency-concept|dependencies]].

handbook.markdown:
The deployment page describes what a deployment runs: Python packages from `requirements.txt` and Node.js packages from `package.json` are installed, a build script runs when `package.json` defines one, and then the command given in app.yaml starts the app. Two files therefore decide what runs: the manifest decides the versions, app.yaml decides the command.

```text
# requirements.txt; synthetic teaching example. Pin every direct dependency
# (fastapi, pydantic, databricks-sdk, databricks-sql-connector, httpx) to the
# version your tests ran against, in the same form as these two:
qa-rules==1.4
cinder-units==3.2
```

```yaml
# app.yaml; synthetic teaching example, checked against the current page. Not deployed.
command: ["uvicorn", "server:app"]   # plus the host and port options the environment page specifies
env:
  - name: QUALITY_WAREHOUSE_ID
    valueFrom: sql-warehouse
```

**Pinning rules** (original guidance): pin every direct dependency to the version the tests used; add a transitive dependency only when a failure proves it matters; keep test-only packages out of the app's manifest; change a pin in its own commit, run the tests, then redeploy.

**The environment ships its own libraries.** The app environment page lists pre-installed packages and the language versions; what your manifest pins is what your code should rely on. A package that happened to be pre-installed can change version with the environment.

**Where the evidence is:** the deployment log's install step shows what was resolved and installed, and the first lines after it show the start command running or failing. An ImportError, a missing module or a version conflict at this point is always a manifest question for the app team, never a permission question.

**Front end builds** follow the same logic: the Node.js packages and the build script run during deployment, so the lockfile the tests used belongs in the repository.

beats.recap: Pin what you tested; the deployment installs the manifest, not your laptop.

beats.title: Validation refuses an injected key before any grant is spent
beats.outcome: Order the checks a request passes, predict what an injection attempt does with and without them, and write the rule for each field.
beats.explanation: The app's principal holds grants the reviewer lacks, so every body is a lever on those grants. [[dbxfe-apps-validation-concept|Request validation]] runs before the handler: a schema with a pattern per field, allowed values, a size limit and no unknown fields; then every value reaches SQL as a bound parameter. Notice in the timeline that sign-in lets the injected key through untouched, the schema refuses it with a 422 naming the field, and neither the warehouse nor Lakebase is called.

samajh.text: Bank mein cheque pehle counter par aata hai. Clerk date, amount aur signature ki jagah dekhta hai; agar amount kaat-peet ke likha hai toh cheque wahin wapas, locker tak koi jaata hi nahi. Aur agar cheque theek bhi ho, toh cashier amount ko bas ek number ki tarah padhta hai, us par likhi kisi 'aur bhi de do' wali line ko nahi maanta.
samajh.mapping: The counter check is request validation with a named reason, the untouched locker is the grant never spent, and reading the amount only as a number is the bound parameter.
samajh.boundary: The counter judges the cheque's form, not whether this customer may draw on that account; permission is the handler's separate check.

handbook.markdown:
```python
# Synthetic teaching example; not executed.
from typing import Literal
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field

class ClaimRequest(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid")          # unknown fields refused
    inspection_key: str = Field(pattern=r"^[A-Z]-\d{4}$")
    revision: int = Field(ge=1, le=999)
    reviewer: str | None = None                        # must match the header if sent

class DispositionRequest(ClaimRequest):
    disposition: Literal["accepted", "corrected", "rejected"]
```

FastAPI answers a body that fails these rules with 422 and a structured `detail` whose `loc` names the field, before the handler runs. Add a request size limit in front of the parser so a megabyte body is refused before anything reads it.

```python
# Parameterized: the value travels separately from the statement text.
cur.execute("SELECT status FROM quality.raw.quarantine "
            "WHERE inspection_key = :key AND revision = :rev",
            {"key": body.inspection_key, "rev": body.revision})
```

**Two layers, two jobs** (original guidance). The schema gives the client a precise refusal and keeps nonsense out of every downstream call; binding guarantees that a value can never become SQL even if a rule is missed. The third state of the timeline shows binding alone: safe, but the client learns nothing about what was wrong.

**The same rule for models and tools.** Text sent to a serving endpoint is data, and a model's reply that proposes a disposition is a proposal: the reviewer still submits it through the same validated request. The tool-authorization module, *Tools, MCP and action authorization*, develops that boundary.

**What to inspect:** a test that posts the injected body and asserts both the 422 and that no fake data service received a call.

beats.recap: Validate shape first, bind every value, and let nothing reach a grant unchecked.

beats.title: Shape, permission and uniqueness are checked in three different places
beats.outcome: Assign each rule to its enforcement point: the schema, the handler's authorization check, or the store's constraint.
beats.explanation: A body can be perfectly shaped and still not be allowed. The schema judges shape. The handler is the [[dbxfe-apps-enforcement-concept|enforcement point]] for permission: is this reviewer a member of the item's plant, since the Lakebase grant belongs to the app, not to Tomas. Lakebase judges uniqueness: one active claim per key and revision, even when two requests race. Notice across the three states which check stops each request, and that the conflict comes back as a normal answer, not an error.

handbook.markdown:
**Why each rule lives where it does** (original guidance): a rule belongs where the facts it needs are visible and cannot be bypassed.

| Rule | Facts needed | Enforcement point |
|---|---|---|
| Key matches `^[A-Z]-\d{4}$` | the body | schema |
| Reviewer belongs to the item's plant | reviewer, plant roster, item | handler |
| One active claim per key and revision | every concurrent write | Lakebase constraint |
| Only the claimant records a disposition | the current claim | Lakebase, checked in the same transaction |
| Dispositions are never updated | the table's grants | Lakebase grants on the app's role |

```python
# Synthetic teaching example; not executed.
@app.post("/v1/claims")
def claim(body: ClaimRequest, request: Request):
    reviewer = reviewer_of(request)
    if body.reviewer not in (None, reviewer):
        raise HTTPException(403, {"reason": "reviewer"})
    if deps.plant_of_item(body.inspection_key) not in deps.plants_of(reviewer):
        raise HTTPException(403, {"reason": "plant"})
    return deps.claims.claim(body.inspection_key, body.revision, reviewer)
```

The store call returns `{"status": "claimed"}` or `{"status": "conflict", "claimed_by": "imani.q"}`; the application state design guide makes the conflict a normal response because two reviewers wanting one item is ordinary business, not a fault.

**Things that are not enforcement points:** a hidden or disabled button (any client can post the body), a check-then-insert in the handler's memory (the race in the check), and a system prompt telling a model to respect plants (a prompt is not access control).

**Unknown, owned:** whether per-reviewer rules could also be enforced inside the database for the app's role is the data lead's question; until it is answered, the handler is the enforcement point and the design note says so. The module *Lakebase, Postgres and operational state* designs and tests the constraints.

beats.recap: Schema for shape, handler for permission, the store for uniqueness.

beats.title: An incident belongs to the layer whose evidence changed
beats.outcome: Match a symptom to its first evidence and owner, and write the order in which an app incident is handed on.
beats.explanation: [[dbxfe-apps-ownership-concept|Operational responsibility]] follows evidence. A failed install is in the deployment log and belongs to the app team; a crash after start is in the app's own log; a denial naming the app's principal is a grant for the data owner; a slow queue starts with the handler's timing and moves to the warehouse owner only when query history shows the wait there. Notice in the second state that the slow-queue incident changes hands once, on evidence, and returns to the app team to verify.

handbook.markdown:
**The owners** (original guidance; adapt the names to the organization):

- **App team:** code, manifest, app.yaml, validation, handler checks, state placement, the app's log content, reviewer-facing errors, deployment and rollback.
- **Data owner:** Unity Catalog grants, row filters and masks on the tables the app reads.
- **Warehouse owner:** sizing, queuing and schedules on the warehouse the app shares.
- **Lakebase owner:** capacity, backups and recovery of the operational store.
- **Secret owner:** rotation of the manuals token, coordinated with the app team's restart.
- **Platform team:** workspace, sign-in and the path to Databricks support.

**Make the evidence exist before the incident.** The app writes one structured line per request: request id, reviewer, route, status and the time spent in each downstream call. Never a token, never a secret, never a whole body.

```python
# Synthetic teaching example; not executed.
# rid: one id per request, set by the app's own middleware
log.info("request", extra={"rid": rid, "reviewer": reviewer, "route": "/v1/queue",
                           "status": 200, "warehouse_ms": 4100, "lakebase_ms": 12})
```

**Decide log retention deliberately.** Where the platform shows an app's logs and how long it keeps them is read from the current documentation; if an audit needs a record of who claimed what, that record is the claim row in Lakebase, not a log line.

**Rollback is part of the runbook:** redeploy the last known good source and confirm with one named reviewer's claim. Record the time, the source revision and the result.

**Why this order matters:** paging the warehouse owner for an ImportError, or rewriting code for a missing grant, spends hours on the wrong layer. Each row of the matrix names the first evidence, and the incident moves only when that evidence points elsewhere.

beats.recap: Read the owning layer's evidence first; hand an incident on only when the evidence moves.

beats.title: A deployment is a replayable sequence, from a folder or a bundle
beats.outcome: Write the deployment sequence for an app from a workspace folder and from a bundle, and label a guide that has not been run as not deployed.
beats.explanation: Syncing files changes nothing a reviewer sees; the [[dbxfe-apps-deployment-concept|deployment]] is what builds and starts the new code. From a workspace folder the sequence is sync, deploy, build, start, verify, share. [[dbxfe-apps-bundle-concept|Declarative Automation Bundles]] declare the app and its resources per target, so the same steps repeat in development and production. Notice that each step in the timeline names its evidence, and that every step is marked pending: a guide nobody has run is labelled not deployed.

handbook.markdown:
```bash
# Not executed in this build; check every flag against the current CLI reference first.
databricks sync ./quality-review /Workspace/Users/<you>/quality-review
databricks apps deploy quality-review \
  --source-code-path /Workspace/Users/<you>/quality-review
```

The deployment page describes this workspace-folder path through the UI or the CLI, and names bundles as another way to define and deploy apps. A bundle is configuration kept beside the code; a schematic shape:

```yaml
# Schematic only: key names are checked against the current bundle reference. Not deployed.
resources:
  apps:
    quality_review:
      name: quality-review
      source_code_path: ./app
targets:
  dev:  {}   # binds wh-quality-dev, quality_ops_dev
  prod: {}   # binds wh-quality, quality_ops
```

Declarative Automation Bundles were formerly named Databricks Asset Bundles; CLI commands keep the `bundle` spelling. The value of a bundle is repetition: the same definition deploys to each target with that target's bindings, and the definition is reviewed like code.

**Verification is part of the deployment** (original guidance): open the URL as a named reviewer, make one test claim, read it back from Lakebase, and read the app log's line for that request. Then share the app with the reviewers' group. Record the deployment id, the source revision and the time.

**Rollback:** redeploy the previous source revision; the rows in Lakebase are untouched by a deployment, so a rollback of code never rolls back claims.

**The label.** Until someone runs the guide and records each result, it is marked *not deployed*. In this course nothing was deployed, no command above was run, and nothing is added to SpicyBrain's own runtime.

beats.recap: Sync, deploy, build, start, verify, share; label it not deployed until it has run.

beats.title: A mocked contract test proves the contract, not the deployment
beats.outcome: Write local mocked contract tests for the app's handlers and state exactly what they prove and what they cannot.
beats.explanation: A [[dbxfe-apps-mock-concept|mocked contract test]] drives the real handler through a local test client with fakes standing in for Lakebase and the plant lookup. Green means the request, response and error contract holds: claimed, conflict, 422 naming the field, 403 for another plant or a mismatched reviewer. Notice which nodes stay excluded after the suite passes: the app's grants, the platform's headers, the build and Postgres under concurrency. A local mock is not a deployed app, and nothing here enters SpicyBrain's own runtime.

samajh.text: Natak ki dress rehearsal mein sab dialogue, entry aur exit check ho jaate hain, par stage par gatte ke props hote hain aur hall ki lights asli show wali nahi. Rehearsal achhi gayi, iska matlab script aur timing theek hai. Iska matlab yeh nahi ki show ke din mic chalega ya audience ke liye seat tayyar hai.
samajh.mapping: The rehearsal is the mocked contract suite, the cardboard props are the fakes, the script and timing are the handler's contract, and the real hall's mic and lights are the grants, headers and build that only a deployment exercises.
samajh.boundary: A rehearsal can be repeated freely, while a deployment check touches shared resources and must be planned, recorded and labelled with what actually ran.

beats.recap: Mocks prove the contract; grants, headers, the build and concurrency need a deployment.

extensionCards.prompt: What does binding a Lakebase database give the app's service principal, and what does it leave for you to grant?
extensionCards.answer: A matching Postgres role named after the principal's client ID, CONNECT and CREATE on the chosen database, and connection variables such as PGHOST; rights on tables it did not create are not included.
extensionCards.explanation: The [[dbxfe-apps-extension-lakebase-role-concept|app Postgres role]] can connect and create objects, so tables the app creates itself are its own. Tables created by a migration job or a data engineer need explicit grants to that role, following the least-privilege grants the Lakebase module tests locally. If a role for the principal already exists the binding reuses it, so read its current grants rather than assuming a clean start. Lakebase availability in the workspace's region is a separate check with its own owner.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Explains why a working Lakebase binding can still meet a permission error on the first query, and which grants the team must add itself.

extensionCards.prompt: If the queue read moves to user authorization, what happens to a Unity Catalog row filter on the quarantine table?
extensionCards.answer: It is evaluated for the signed-in reviewer, so each reviewer sees only the rows the filter admits; under app authorization the same filter is evaluated for the app's principal instead.
extensionCards.explanation: A [[dbxfe-apps-extension-row-filters-concept|row filter under user authorization]] follows the principal that runs the query. Written as a per-plant rule, it narrows Imani's queue to P2 only when the warehouse call carries her token; under app authorization it must admit the app's principal or the app sees nothing, and the handler does the narrowing. Filters are query-time visibility controls with documented limits on supported access paths, so confirm the warehouse path is covered, test with reviewers from two plants and read the principal in query history.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Shows how moving one request to user authorization changes where per-plant visibility is enforced, and what to test before trusting it.

extensionCards.prompt: What does a deployment do with a Node.js front end whose package.json defines a build script?
extensionCards.answer: It installs the Node.js packages listed in package.json and runs the build script before the app's start command runs, so the built front end comes from the deployment itself.
extensionCards.explanation: A [[dbxfe-apps-extension-node-build-concept|front-end build at deployment]] lets a React or Svelte front end be compiled from source during each deployment instead of being committed as built files. A failing build ends that deployment before the start command runs, and the deployment log shows the failing step; check on the current page what the app serves while a deployment fails. Keep the lockfile your tests used in the repository, and read how combined Python and Node.js projects are ordered before relying on it.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Connects the documented deployment steps to front-end frameworks, where a missing or failing build step is a common first-deployment surprise.

extensionCards.prompt: Why can a local run of the app read the quarantine table while the deployed app is refused?
extensionCards.answer: Locally no app credentials are injected, so the SDK authenticates with the developer's own login; deployed, the injected app credentials make the app's service principal the caller, with its own grants.
extensionCards.explanation: DATABRICKS_CLIENT_ID and DATABRICKS_CLIENT_SECRET are injected into the app's environment, not into a laptop. Locally the SDK falls back to the [[dbxfe-apps-extension-local-identity-concept|local developer identity]], usually a personal profile with broader grants than the app will ever hold, so a local success says nothing about the app's principal. Read the principal in query history for both runs, grant the app's principal exactly what the design needs, and treat the first deployed request as the real permission test.
extensionCards.whyItMatters: Explains the most common works-locally, fails-deployed permission surprise and the evidence that tells the two identities apart.

recap.title: One request, three boundaries, an identity per hop
recap.markdown: **A browser reaches the app; only the back end reaches data, models and tools.** Every hop has an identity: the reviewer at sign-in, the platform's forwarded headers as user context, and at each data hop either the app's own service principal or, under user authorization bounded by scopes, the reviewer's token. Resources bind a permission and a variable; secrets are read at start and never printed; state lives where it must survive, with operational records in Lakebase; request validation runs before any grant is spent, the handler enforces permission and the store enforces uniqueness. A mocked contract test proves the contract, and a guide nobody has run is labelled not deployed. **Transfer challenge:** redraw the identity table for a supplier-returns app whose suppliers hold no Databricks identity, marking which hops could use user authorization, where the supplier's identity would be recorded, and which facts you would verify before the design review.

appliedTask.title: Add suggestions and a second plant without moving state or trust
appliedTask.prompt: Cinderline adds East Yard (P3) reviewers and wants the disposition-suggest serving endpoint to propose a disposition beside each queue item. The data lead has now added a per-plant row filter to quality.raw.quarantine, and the platform team says the app may run on more than one process. Update the blueprint: the identity at each hop for view queue, suggestion and record disposition; the new resource row; how a suggestion is validated and where it is kept, if anywhere; two new mocked contract tests shown as Python and labelled not executed here; and the changes to the deployment guide, labelled not deployed. Nothing is added to SpicyBrain's own runtime.
appliedTask.modelAnswer: View queue: the warehouse read moves to the reviewer's forwarded token with the sql scope, so the new row filter decides which quarantine rows each reviewer sees, P3 reviewers included; before the switch the reviewers' group, P3 included, is granted USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and SELECT on quality.raw.quarantine, and warehouse access is confirmed with its owner, or every reviewer's queue fails with a permission error; claims still come from Lakebase as the app, narrowed by the handler, and a missing token is refused rather than falling back to the app. Suggestion: the back end calls disposition-suggest as the app's principal, bound with Can query and read through SUGGEST_ENDPOINT; the reply is data, checked against the allowed dispositions and shown labelled as a suggestion, never written as a disposition. Record disposition: unchanged, written by the app's role after the claimant check, with the reviewer taken from the header. Suggestions are a cache keyed by inspection key and revision with an expiry, so another process simply recomputes. Tests, shown and not executed here: a fake endpoint replying 'scrapped' is refused as outside the allowed values and nothing is shown; a P3 reviewer's claim on a P3 item succeeds while Tomas from P1 still receives 403. Guide changes, not deployed: bind the endpoint, confirm user authorization status, the row filter and the reviewers' grants with their owners, deploy, and verify that one newly added P3 reviewer sees P3 rows, not an error, by reading the principal in query history.
appliedTask.reasoning: The answer changes identity only at the hop whose data now carries per-user rules, treats model output as untrusted data behind the same validation as a request, keeps every shared fact out of process memory so more processes change capacity rather than correctness, and labels tests and deployment honestly.
